issues.legal_issue: The repeal and re-enactment of ceiling legislation did not prevent pending ceiling proceedings from being decided under the repealed law where the new legislation did not manifest a contrary intention.
material_facts: The earlier tenancy legislation imposed a ceiling on agricultural holdings and provided for determination with reference to a notified date.

The later ceiling legislation repealed the earlier ceiling provisions but included provisions preserving certain applications of the old law, including reopening specified decided matters and retaining the old ceiling standard in certain circumstances.
After the later legislation came into force, ceiling proceedings under the earlier law were initiated or continued against landholders.
The landholders argued that the differences between the two statutory schemes and the later law’s overriding clause prevented use of the repealed law in pending cases.
issues.conclusion: Pending ceiling proceedings could be initiated or continued under the repealed provisions because the later legislation did not manifest an intention inconsistent with saving the old law for those proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 6 of the Rajasthan General Clauses Act, 1955, repeal does not affect accrued rights, incurred liabilities, or proceedings concerning them unless a different intention appears. When repeal is accompanied by re-enactment on the same subject, the new enactment must be examined to determine whether it manifests that different intention; mere omission of an express reference to section 6 is not conclusive. A saving clause is not exhaustive of rights and obligations that survive repeal. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh, B. Bansgopal v. Emperor, Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh, Chief Inspector of Mines v. K.C. Thapar, and I.T. Commissioner, U.P. v. Shah Sadiq and Sons. It found that sections 15(2) and 40(1), read with the second proviso to section 4(1) of the 1973 Act, showed no contrary intention; section 3’s reference to law for the time being in force did not exclude a law deemed to remain in force.

rule.if: ceiling_proceeding_under_repealed_law and pending_when_repealed and repeal_followed_by_reenactment and new_law_preserved_some_application_of_old_law and not contrary_intention_in_new_law

predicates.ceiling_proceeding_under_repealed_law: A proceeding to determine a ceiling on agricultural holdings was brought under an earlier law.
predicates.pending_when_repealed: The proceeding had not been concluded when the earlier law was repealed.
predicates.repeal_followed_by_reenactment: The legislature repealed the earlier law and enacted a replacement law on the same subject.
predicates.new_law_preserved_some_application_of_ol: The replacement law retained specified applications or remedies under the earlier law.
predicates.contrary_intention_in_new_law: The replacement law’s provisions manifest an intention inconsistent with applying the earlier law to pending proceedings.

issues.definition: When a ceiling proceeding under an earlier law remains pending at repeal, and the replacement law preserves some applications of that law without manifesting a contrary intention, the earlier law governs the pending proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A State’s right to excess agricultural land and a landholder’s liability to surrender it accrued under the earlier ceiling law when the holding exceeded the ceiling on the relevant appointed date, even if quantification and transfer of possession occurred later.
material_facts: The earlier law prohibited a person from retaining agricultural land in excess of the applicable ceiling as from a notified date and required surrender of excess land.
The applicable ceiling and excess holding were to be determined by reference to the notified date.
The later legislation repealed the earlier ceiling provisions while proceedings to determine excess holdings remained pending.
The State argued that its right and the landholder’s liability arose only after completion of the proceedings and identification of the land to be surrendered.
issues.conclusion: The State’s right to the excess land had accrued, and the landholder’s liability to surrender it had been incurred, as of the notified date; later quantification did not prevent those rights and liabilities from surviving repeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(c) and (e) of the Rajasthan General Clauses Act, 1955, preserve accrued rights and incurred liabilities, and proceedings concerning them, after repeal unless a different intention appears. Under section 30E of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, the prohibition on holding land above the ceiling and the obligation to report and surrender excess land operated by reference to the notified date. The right and liability therefore arose on that date even though quantification remained to be worked out. The Court relied on Lalji Raja v. Firm Hansraj, Raghunath v. Maharashtra, Bhikoba Shankar Dhumal v. Mohan Lal Punchand Tathed, State of Maharashtra v. Annapurnabai, Director of Public Works v. Ho Po Sang, and M.S. Shivananda v. K.S.R. Corpn.

rule.if: ceiling_proceeding_under_repealed_law and excess_holding_measured_on_appointed_date and obligation_to_surrender_excess_arose_on_that_date and quantification_remained_after_that_date

predicates.ceiling_proceeding_under_repealed_law: A proceeding to determine a ceiling on agricultural holdings was brought under an earlier law.
predicates.excess_holding_measured_on_appointed_dat: The law measured whether a holding exceeded the ceiling by reference to a specified appointed or notified date.
predicates.obligation_to_surrender_excess_arose_on_: The law required a person holding excess land on that date to surrender it to the State.
predicates.quantification_remained_after_that_date: The amount of excess land or its identification remained to be determined after the specified date.

issues.definition: Where an earlier ceiling law measures excess holdings and creates a surrender obligation as of a specified date, the State’s right and the landholder’s liability survive repeal even if quantification remains outstanding.
